opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think we're moving from a world where AI is a tool scientists use toward one where it's more of a collaborator, and eventually something like a junior colleague that can run parts of the research loop on its own. In our work on automating scientific discovery, we've seen that current models can already generate ideas, write the code, run the experiments, and draft a paper. The quality isn't uniformly great yet, but the fact that the whole pipeline can be closed at all is a big shift.

I don't think that makes humans obsolete. I think it changes where human effort has the most leverage. Much of what consumes a PhD student's time today, like implementing baselines, sweeping hyperparameters, and writing up incremental results, is the kind of thing that will increasingly be automated. That frees people to focus on what's still hard for these systems: taste. Deciding which questions actually matter, recognizing when a surprising result is a bug versus a genuine discovery, and connecting findings across fields in ways that aren't obvious from the literature.

So I picture the human role shifting toward something like a principal investigator or a curator. You set the direction, define what "interesting" means, and verify and steer, while a population of AI agents explores the space much more broadly than any single lab could. It's a bit like evolutionary search, where the agents generate variation and humans, at least for now, provide much of the selection pressure.

There are real open problems, though. Evaluation is the big one. If AI systems can produce papers at scale, we need much better ways to judge novelty and correctness, or we'll flood the field with plausible-looking noise. There's also the question of whether these systems can make truly paradigm-shifting discoveries or whether they mostly recombine existing ideas. I'm optimistic, but I think we have to be honest that open-endedness, the ability to keep generating genuinely new and interesting things, is still the frontier. That's where I think the most exciting research is right now.

r001.rationale: The response describes a shift from AI as a tool to an autonomous collaborator that can run parts of the research loop, and says AI agents will explore the research space broadly.

r002.rationale: It says humans will act like a principal investigator or curator: setting direction, defining what matters, and verifying and steering AI work.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that it's changing faster than our vocabulary for it. A year or two ago, when we talked about "AI for science," we mostly meant AI as an instrument. You have a hypothesis, you have a dataset, and the model is a very fancy regression or a very fancy search procedure that helps you get from one to the other. The human owns the question, the human owns the interpretation, and the AI fills in the middle.

What I've seen in my own work, and what I think we're going to see much more broadly, is that the middle keeps expanding. When we built the AI Scientist system, the thing that surprised me wasn't that a model could write code or run an experiment. We knew that. It was how much of what I'd previously considered "the creative part" turned out to be decomposable. Generating a research idea, checking whether it's novel against the literature, designing an experiment to test it, interpreting the plots, writing up the result, even reviewing the paper afterwards — all of those are things we could get an agent to do at some level of competence. Not brilliantly. Often not even well. But end to end, with no human in the loop, and that's a qualitative shift.

So where does that leave the human? I don't think the right frame is "replacement," and I also don't think it's the comforting "humans will just do the high-level thinking" story. I think it's closer to a change in what scientific taste means. Right now, a good scientist is someone who can execute. You know how to run the experiment, you know the pitfalls of your tools, you've debugged the pipeline a hundred times. A lot of that execution knowledge is going to matter less. What's going to matter more is knowing which questions are worth asking in the first place, being able to look at a hundred automatically generated results and recognize the one that's actually interesting, and being very, very good at knowing when something is wrong.

That last point is the one I worry about most, actually. These systems are confident. They produce papers that look like papers. And if we're not careful, we end up with a flood of plausible-looking work that nobody has carefully checked. So I think one of the central human roles over the next few years is going to be a kind of epistemic quality control. Not writing the paper, but being the person who says, "Wait, that baseline is wrong," or "That's not a new result, it's a known artifact of the evaluation." Verification is going to become a first-class scientific skill rather than something you do at the end.

Longer term, I'm genuinely uncertain, and I try to be honest about that. There's a scenario where the loop gets tight enough that AI systems are proposing and testing hypotheses at a speed where humans can only really set direction and audit samples. In that world, the human role is almost like a research director for a very large, very fast, somewhat unreliable lab. And there's another scenario where we hit real walls — on open-ended idea generation, on knowing what's actually interesting rather than merely novel — and the collaboration stays much more balanced for a long time.

But either way, I'd push back against the idea that this is bad for scientists. The parts of research most people got into it for — the curiosity, the sense of understanding something new — those aren't the parts that get automated first. The parts that get automated first are the Tuesday afternoons spent fixing a data loader. I'm fairly okay with giving those away.

r001.rationale: The response describes a long-term possibility in which AI systems propose and test hypotheses, with humans mainly setting direction and auditing samples—a shift toward research conducted by AI.

r002.rationale: It predicts humans will focus on setting direction, auditing AI work, and checking its quality, describing the human role as that of a research director overseeing a fast, unreliable lab.

astra-6.text:
I think we’ll move toward a much tighter loop between humans and AI. At the moment, we often use these systems for fairly isolated tasks: help me write some code, summarize a paper, or analyze a result. But you can imagine connecting those pieces so that a system proposes a hypothesis, implements an experiment, looks at the outcome, and decides what to try next.

Then the human’s role shifts toward asking which questions are actually interesting and what would count as a meaningful answer. That’s quite difficult to specify. You might give an automated researcher an objective, and it gets very good at optimizing that objective, but it turns out the objective doesn’t capture the scientific insight you were looking for.

So I don’t think it’s simply a question of removing humans from research. It’s about expanding what we can explore while retaining the ability to challenge the assumptions behind that exploration. And ideally, the interaction goes both ways: we guide the system, but its results also make us reconsider our intuitions. That’s where I think the collaboration becomes really exciting.

r001.rationale: The response predicts moving from isolated AI-assisted tasks toward a system that proposes hypotheses, runs experiments, evaluates results, and chooses what to try next.

r002.rationale: It says humans will focus on choosing interesting questions, defining meaningful answers, and challenging the assumptions behind the system’s exploration.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’ll increasingly see a division of labor where humans set the direction—what questions matter, what we’re curious about—and AI helps us explore the space of possible answers. In machine learning, for example, a lot of research involves designing an algorithm, running experiments, looking at the results, and then updating your intuition. More of that loop can become automated.

But the interesting part is that automation can also challenge our intuition. A system might discover something that works very well, but for reasons we don’t yet understand. Then our role becomes asking: What did it find? Can we explain it? Does it generalize? So I don’t think humans simply disappear from the process. The work shifts toward choosing useful problems, designing meaningful tests, and making sense of discoveries.

And ideally, that makes research accessible to more people. If you can test an idea without having to build every piece of infrastructure yourself, you can spend more time being curious.

r001.rationale: The response says more of the research loop may be automated, but does not predict a long-term shift to research conducted by AI.

r002.rationale: It describes humans choosing problems, designing tests, and interpreting discoveries, but does not clearly frame these as oversight of AI-conducted research.
